newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguay's chamber of deputies okays bank reform.
newsitem.headline: Paraguay's chamber of deputies okays bank reform.

text.p: Paraguay's Lower House of Congress passed a "financial emergency" law Friday to mitigate the effects of a banking crisis which shook the country in June.
The law, which still needs approval by the Senate, would fully guarantee personal checking accounts and would guarantee savings deposits for up to $11,500.

Social security funds deposited in banks would be fully reimbursed by the state if a bank folded or were wound up, while funds belonging to other government departments would be 50 percent reimbursed. The emergency law was passed 40 days after Paraguay faced its second banking crisis in two years, which ended with the government taking control in June of Banco Union, the country's largest private bank.

The rescue plan proposed by President Juan Carlos Wasmosy's administration has triggered rows between legislators who support the use of public funds in this way and those who denounce it, warning of fraud and corruption.

"It's shameful that Congress will consent to give public funds to swindlers and help out a government linked to them," opposition deputy Paraguayo Cubas told reporters after the bill was approved. Another opposition deputy, Marcelo Duarte, said the lower house "tried to do the best it could to overcome a critical situation."

The recent banking scandal led to the resignation for "ethical reasons" of Industry Minister Ubaldo Scavone, accused of covering up problems at Banco Union, which was controlled by his family. The government before that had acknowledged it knew of irregularities in banks as early as two years ago.
Paraguay has been in the grips of a financial crisis since May 1995, which according to official data required, up to June, the injection of almost $500 million in funds.
The Central Bank said in its report to Congress that the guarantee system proposed by the new law would mean setting aside another $1.1 billion for contingency purposes.

Those funds, which represent 60 percent of the entire budget of the central government administration, would guarantee deposits at Paraguay's 28 banks and 56 other financial institutions that handle personal accounts.
